section_summary: This section covers late January through mid-February 1937, documenting the political crisis triggered by the fall of the Hirota Cabinet and intense army opposition that blocked General Kazushige Ugaki from forming a new government. General Senjuro Hayashi subsequently formed a transitional, non-party cabinet composed of moderate officers and bureaucrats, with banker Toyotaro Yuki at Finance to calm economic anxieties and General Hajime Sugiyama soon replacing Kotaro Nakamura as War Minister. Diplomatic dispatches trace Premier Hayashi's foreign policy pronouncements as well as Ambassador Joseph C. Grew's comprehensive annual survey examining Japan's international isolation, non-treaty naval status, strained relations with China, the USSR, and Great Britain, and growing domestic friction over military spending and economic controls.

subfiles.about: Reports persistent Japanese Army opposition preventing General Ugaki from appointing a War Minister and outlines potential outcomes if he fails to form a cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that military opposition to General Kazushige Ugaki remains firm, with the army indicating it will refuse to nominate a Minister of War to serve in his proposed cabinet. Ugaki has not yet reported his failure to the Throne, but observers anticipate three alternatives if he cannot proceed: the Emperor might reject his resignation and compel the army to nominate a minister, Prince Konoye might be commanded to form a cabinet, or General Minami might be chosen.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 29 from Tokyo Regarding Army Opposition to Ugaki Cabinet

subfiles.about: Reports on General Ugaki's Palace conference with the Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal and growing high-level resistance to army political dictation.
keywords: Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that General Ugaki conferred at the Palace for over an hour with Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal Kurahei Yuasa, subsequently announcing he would continue his effort to form a cabinet with Court backing. An accompanying Department paraphrase underscores that Court officials were displeased with the military's obstruction. Grew notes that tension among prominent Japanese figures reflects the most determined resistance against military political dictation seen in fifteen years.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 30 from Tokyo Regarding Ugaki's Palace Conference and Resistance to Army Dictation

subfiles.about: Analyzes the clash between political parties and the military following the prorogation of the Diet and the resignation of the Hirota Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs assesses the prorogation of the Diet and the subsequent resignation of the Hirota Cabinet amid intense party resistance to the military. While American press observers attribute the collapse primarily to economic strains from heavy defense spending, Dooman emphasizes public discontent with the China policy, the Anti-Comintern Pact with Germany, and poor relations with the US, Britain, and the USSR. He concludes that while liberal opposition to army dominance is expanding, it will take considerable time to mature.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Eugene H. Dooman on the Parliamentary Crisis in Japan

subfiles.about: Reports General Ugaki's formal report of failure to the Emperor, his resignation from the retired army list, and speculation on his successor.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that General Ugaki formally notified the Throne of his inability to form a cabinet, leaving Baron Hiranuma and Admiral Osumi as the leading contenders to succeed him. Before proceeding to the Palace, Ugaki and retired General Hayashi released statements sharply criticizing military interference in politics. Although Japanese authorities placed a press ban on the statements, correspondent Wilfrid Fleisher telephoned the complete texts to the New York Herald Tribune.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 33 from Tokyo Regarding Ugaki's Failure to Form a Cabinet

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for a memorandum discussing the political conflict between the Hirota Cabinet and the Japanese Diet.
subfiles.summary: A State Department document file note cross-referencing a memorandum dated January 23, 1937, by John Carter Vincent of the Far Eastern Division. The memorandum analyzes the situation in the Far East, specifically discussing the conflict between the Hirota Cabinet and the Japanese Diet. The original paper is filed under decimal file 893.00/13949.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Conflict Between the Hirota Cabinet and the Diet

subfiles.about: Reports the designation of retired General Senjuro Hayashi as Premier and analyzes the political and economic implications of his upcoming administration.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that after Baron Hiranuma declined the premiership, retired General Senjuro Hayashi was selected to form a cabinet, marking a victory for the military. Hayashi is described as a moderate, disciplined soldier opposed to army political involvement, chosen to reduce friction between the armed forces and the government. The anticipated cabinet is expected to adopt the army's continental policy and defense programs, prompting anxiety among industrialists and financiers over increased economic controls and inflation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 34 from Tokyo Regarding Selection of General Senjuro Hayashi as Premier

subfiles.about: Briefs the Secretary of State on the Japanese parliamentary crisis and General Ugaki's designation ahead of a meeting with the Japanese Ambassador.
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Eugene H. Dooman
subfiles.summary: Stanley K. Hornbeck submits a briefing and an attached analysis by Eugene H. Dooman regarding the Japanese parliamentary crisis for Secretary Hull's upcoming interview with Ambassador Saito. Dooman details the army's demand for Diet dissolution, the navy's refusal to support an open break with political parties, and Prince Saionji's advice recommending General Ugaki. The memo characterizes Ugaki as a moderate liberal acceptable to the Minseito, while noting that even a constitutional cabinet is unlikely to substantially reduce military estimates or alter core foreign policy.
subfiles.title: Memoranda by Stanley K. Hornbeck and Eugene H. Dooman on the Japanese Parliamentary Crisis

subfiles.about: Reports the installation and roster of the Hayashi Cabinet and transmits the report for the confidential information of the Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports the formal installation of the Hayashi Cabinet, listing ministerial appointments including Premier Hayashi concurrently holding Foreign Affairs and Education, Kotaro Nakamura at War, Mitsumasa Yonai at Navy, and Toyotaro Yuki at Finance and Overseas Affairs. Public and financial anxiety was substantially relieved by the selection of moderate figures, especially Yuki, an experienced banker expected to avoid Baba's inflationary financing. A copy of the telegram was transmitted to the Secretary of the Treasury on February 3, 1937.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 36 from Tokyo Regarding Installation of the Hayashi Cabinet and Transmittal to Treasury

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for a memorandum assessing General Hayashi's selection as a concession to the military.
subfiles.summary: A State Department document file note referencing a memorandum dated January 30, 1937, by John Carter Vincent of the Far Eastern Division. The memorandum evaluates political developments in Japan following General Ugaki's failure to form a cabinet due to army obstruction. It notes that Hayashi's selection represents a concession to the military, ensuring his cabinet formation efforts will not be blocked, with the original filed under 893.00/13961.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Hayashi's Cabinet Formation as a Concession to the Army

subfiles.about: Analyzes the political composition, vague platform, and transitional nature of the Hayashi Cabinet, including Department paraphrases and transmittal to Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew characterizes the Hayashi Cabinet as a moderate, transitional administration formed because military leaders recognized public backlash against their role in ousting Hirota and blocking Ugaki. The government lacks party affiliation and presents vague platform commitments concerning national polity, industrial development, and defense repletion. Grew identifies Finance Minister Yuki as the cabinet's strong figure following Takahashi's conservative financial principles, while noting the replacement of Itagaki with Nakamura and the emergence of a reactionary party under General Tatekawa, with departmental paraphrases and an informational memorandum transmitted to Secretary Morgenthau.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 43 from Tokyo on the Character and Policies of the Hayashi Cabinet, with Paraphrase and Treasury Transmittal

subfiles.about: Reports the official announcement of the Hayashi Cabinet's five general policy principles.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that the Hayashi Cabinet formally announced five general policies, four of which elaborate on earlier statements regarding constitutional administration, clarification of national polity, defense repletion, and diplomatic policy, while the fifth promotes national welfare through industrial encouragement. Grew remarks that the statement is framed in nebulous language that does not justify cabling full details, which will follow by dispatch. An attached confidential departmental paraphrase records the message.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 49 from Tokyo Regarding the Official Policy Announcement of the Hayashi Cabinet

subfiles.about: Analyzes the installation, ministerial personnel, and background of General Hayashi's new cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Eugene H. Dooman analyzes the installation of General Hayashi's cabinet, reviewing Hayashi's career including his actions in the 1931 Mukden Incident, his tenure replacing General Araki as War Minister, and his post-February 26 Incident retirement. The memorandum notes that allocating ten portfolios among seven non-party ministers reflects military pressure for administrative reform, while reviewing appointments such as Admiral Yonai at Navy, Nakamura at War, and Yuki at Finance. Dooman also discounts press reports that Ambassador Hirosi Saito will be appointed Foreign Minister.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Eugene H. Dooman on the Hayashi Cabinet Crisis and Appointments

subfiles.about: Reports key personnel shifts in Japan's War Ministry and Bank of Japan, including Department paraphrases and informational transmittal to the Treasury.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports significant leadership changes: General Hajime Sugiyama succeeded Kotaro Nakamura as War Minister due to the latter's illness, while former War Minister Terauchi assumed Sugiyama's previous role as Inspector-General of Military Training, strengthening army influence over the budget. Simultaneously, Eigo Fukai resigned as Governor of the Bank of Japan and was replaced by Seihin Ikeda of Mitsui, with Juichi Tsushima named Vice Governor. These appointments formed an influential financial triumvirate with Yuki, and the details were forwarded via memorandum to the Secretary of the Treasury on February 10.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 52 from Tokyo Regarding Key Military and Financial Appointments, with Paraphrase and Treasury Transmittal

subfiles.about: Cross-reference note for a weekly memorandum reviewing developments in the Japanese cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: A State Department document file note referencing a memorandum dated February 6, 1937, by John Carter Vincent of the Far Eastern Division. The memorandum summarizes weekly developments concerning the cabinet crisis and general political situation in Japan. The original document is filed under decimal file 893.00/13970.
subfiles.title: Document File Note Regarding Far Eastern Developments and the Japanese Cabinet Crisis

subfiles.about: Reports Premier Hayashi's address before the House of Peers discussing budget policies and foreign relations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on Premier Hayashi's placatory address to the House of Peers, which indicated a desire to cooperate with the Diet and explained proposed tax increases and budget revisions. On foreign affairs, Hayashi advocated closer cooperation and mutual assistance with China, adopted a firm tone toward Soviet Russia while defending the German-Japanese Anti-Comintern Pact, and reiterated immutable friendship with Britain and the United States. Foreign Office spokesman Eiji Amau confirmed to Grew that Hayashi intentionally omitted mention of pending US-Japan issues to signal satisfactory bilateral relations.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 57 from Tokyo Regarding Premier Hayashi's Address to the House of Peers

subfiles.about: Presents an exhaustive annual survey of foreign relations, domestic politics, military and naval status, and economic conditions facing Japan at the start of 1937.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew submits an extensive survey analyzing Japan's strategic and political position at the opening of 1937. The report reviews relations with the United States, China, the Soviet Union, Germany, Italy, Great Britain, and the Netherlands, highlighting Japan's increasing international isolation and the repercussions of dual civilian-military control of foreign policy. It examines rising public criticism of military dominance, the non-treaty status resulting from the expiration of naval limitation treaties, expansion of armed forces budgets, and impending economic strains from price inflation, tax increases, and proposed quasi-wartime state control of key industries.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2209 from Tokyo: General Situation Facing Japan at the Opening of the Year 1937
